name: Sermorelin
lead: Sermorelin (sermorelin acetate; brand names Geref and Gerel) is a synthetic peptide made of the first 29 amino acids of human growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), thought to be the shortest fully active fragment of the natural 44-amino-acid hormone. It binds the GHRH receptor on the pituitary gland and prompts release of the body's own growth hormone (GH).[1][2]

The US Food and Drug Administration approved sermorelin in 1997 as a diagnostic agent for growth hormone secretion and as a treatment for children with growth hormone deficiency or growth failure. The manufacturer discontinued production in 2008 for commercial reasons not related to safety, and it is no longer available as an approved commercial product, though it can still be obtained through compounding pharmacies and prescribed off label.[1][2]

In recent years sermorelin has been promoted by telehealth and wellness clinics for age-related decline, body composition and recovery. Reviews describe its hormonal mechanism as real but note limited controlled evidence of visible body-composition or cosmetic benefit in healthy adults, and it is prohibited in competitive sport.[1][2][5][7]

paras: Sermorelin was developed as a truncated synthetic analogue of GHRH and introduced mainly as a diagnostic tool for growth hormone secretion in children with suspected deficiency. It was also used to treat children with growth hormone deficiency or growth failure by stimulating the pituitary to release GH, increasing plasma GH levels.[1] A published review covers its use in the diagnosis and treatment of children with idiopathic growth hormone deficiency.[11]

Wikipedia notes that clinical adoption remained limited compared with other endocrine testing methods, and that its use declined in the early 2000s as alternative diagnostic strategies and recombinant hormone assays became more widely available.[1]

Sermorelin binds the GHRH receptor and mimics the effect of the full-length hormone in promoting GH secretion. Its effect remains subject to negative feedback by somatostatin, which Wikipedia describes as making overdose difficult compared with injected recombinant GH and as prompting pulsatile rather than constant GH release.[1] Wikipedia's account adds that sermorelin is said to stimulate GH gene transcription and so support the pituitary axis in ageing, while noting that no conclusive results exist on adult benefit.[1]

A review of PEGylated GRF analogues states that native GRF(1-29), the sermorelin sequence, keeps bioactivity in vitro and is almost as effective as the full hormone at eliciting GH secretion in vivo, but has a short plasma half-life of about 10 to 20 minutes in humans because of kidney filtration and enzymatic degradation at its N-terminus.[6] The review presents PEGylation as one approach to obtaining longer-lived forms.[6]
Published human work on sermorelin consists mainly of older pediatric diagnostic and treatment studies, with limited controlled data in healthy or ageing adults.

Children: A review of sermorelin's use in diagnosing and treating idiopathic growth hormone deficiency in children summarises the studies that supported its approval.[11] A study of the physiology of GH in pregnancy administered sermorelin to five pregnant women at term before cesarean section to examine maternal and fetal pituitary and placental GH secretion.[10]

Adults and ageing: A narrative review of GH secretagogues in hypogonadal men says all of the compounds it covers, including sermorelin, are potent GH and IGF-1 stimulators that can improve body composition, but states that data on their clinical efficacy remain limited.[7] A 2026 review of peptides in urology and sexual medicine notes that GH secretagogues reliably increase GH but that clinical evidence is limited.[8] Wikipedia states there are no conclusive results on whether sermorelin yields benefits in adults such as enhancing pituitary function.[1]

Registered trials: ClinicalTrials.gov lists studies of GHRH, the class to which sermorelin belongs, in elderly adults, in healthy men, in abdominal obesity, in HIV-associated lipodystrophy, in congestive heart failure and in mild cognitive impairment, several of them small or terminated early.[13][14][15][16][17][18][19]
No published randomized trial has tested sermorelin for cosmetic outcomes in healthy adults.

Grokipedia lists injection-site reactions as the most common adverse effect, with rarer headache and flushing, and notes that long-term safety data in adults are limited; it also states that growth hormone therapies in general carry potential risks such as joint pain, diabetes risk and cancer concerns.[2]

Reviews of peptides in sport and bodybuilding warn that evidence of benefit is limited, that studies examine controlled therapeutic dosing rather than the combined protocols used in physique culture, and that unregulated supply chains can yield mislabeled or contaminated products.[5][4]

Sermorelin was developed in the late twentieth century during research into peptide regulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. The FDA approved it in 1997, and Geref production ended in 2008 for commercial reasons.[1][2] Grokipedia adds that the new drug applications were withdrawn in 2009 and that the compound remains eligible for generic approval.[2] Since then it has been compounded by pharmacies under US rules for individual prescriptions.[2]

Wikipedia notes that sermorelin can be prescribed off label without the legal restrictions that apply to recombinant growth hormone, which has fuelled use in anti-ageing and performance-enhancement settings.[1][2] Anti-ageing clinics promote improved skin elasticity, reduced wrinkles and better hair growth, but sources cited in one summary say there is limited scientific evidence for such effects in healthy adults.[2] Peptide reviews list sermorelin among GHRH analogues used in sport and bodybuilding and note that WADA prohibits GHRH analogues, with analytical methods developed to detect sermorelin and related peptides.[5][9]
